query: What does this passage say about A retrieval pipeline for evidence-grounded answers?
positive_text:
# A retrieval pipeline for evidence-grounded answers

A retrieval-augmented answer has two stages. First, a retriever selects passages that may support the question. Second, a language model drafts an answer from those passages. The retrieved passages should remain attached to the answer so a reader can inspect the evidence. This keeps retrieval errors visible: a fluent paragraph does not prove that the right source was found.

For a small research assistant, keep the pipeline explicit: ingest source files, assign stable chunk IDs, retrieve a candidate set, optionally rerank it, and ask the writer to use only that evidence. If the candidate set is empty or does not support the requested detail, the system should say so instead of filling gaps from model memory.
negative_text:
# Hybrid retrieval combines independent candidate lists

A hybrid retriever runs more than one search method for the same question. A common pairing is dense semantic search and sparse lexical search. Dense search can surface a paraphrase, while lexical search can preserve a rare token or exact code. The combined candidate pool is then ordered by a fusion rule.

Fusion cannot recover a passage that none of the component searches returned. Candidate depth therefore matters: each retrieval leg must pass enough plausible results into the fusion stage. Evaluate the full pipeline on labeled questions; a hybrid label by itself does not demonstrate better retrieval.

Reference: [Qdrant hybrid queries](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/search/hybrid-queries/); [Qdrant text hybrid search](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/search/text-search/hybrid-search/).

query: What does this passage say about Dense and lexical search find different evidence?
positive_text:
# Dense and lexical search find different evidence

Lexical search compares query terms with terms in the document. It is useful for exact names, codes, uncommon phrases, and version strings. Its weakness is vocabulary mismatch: a passage can express the same idea with different words and receive little lexical signal.

Dense search embeds a query and passages, then looks for nearby vectors. It can connect related wording, but a close vector match may still miss a precise identifier or treat two different numbers as similar. These methods make different errors, so a hybrid system can retrieve with both and combine their ranked candidates.

Reference: [Sentence Transformers retrieve and rerank](https://sbert.net/examples/applications/retrieve_rerank/README.html); [Qdrant text hybrid search](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/search/text-search/hybrid-search/).

# Reciprocal Rank Fusion

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combines ranked lists using the positions of shared candidates rather than adding raw scores. With one-indexed ranks, a common form is `score(d) = Σ 1 / (k + rank(d))`, summed over result lists where document `d` appears. The constant `k` controls how quickly lower ranks lose influence.

This is helpful when retrievers use score scales that do not mean the same thing. A cosine similarity and a BM25 score should not be added as if one unit represented the same evidence strength in both systems. RRF still depends on the component rankings and candidate cutoffs, so record those settings during evaluation.

Reference: [Qdrant hybrid query fusion](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/search/hybrid-queries/).

# NDCG rewards relevant passages near the top

Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) evaluates a ranked list when relevance labels can have multiple grades. It gives more weight to items near the top, discounts items farther down, then normalizes by the score of an ideal ordering. This makes values from different queries more comparable than raw discounted gain alone.

NDCG complements recall and reciprocal rank. Recall measures how much of the known relevant set was retrieved; reciprocal rank focuses on the first relevant item; NDCG considers the ordering of graded relevance. Choose the cutoff `k` to match the number of passages the application actually presents or uses.

Reference: [scikit-learn `ndcg_score`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.metrics.ndcg_score.html).

query: What does this passage say about Fusion choices need an empirical comparison?
positive_text:
# Fusion choices need an empirical comparison

RRF uses rank positions and discards score magnitudes. Distribution-Based Score Fusion (DBSF) instead normalizes score distributions within each result list before combining them. The two methods preserve different information: RRF is less sensitive to incompatible scales, while distribution-based fusion lets relative score gaps affect the result.

Neither rule is guaranteed to win for every corpus. Compare them on the same held-out questions, using the same component retrievers, candidate depths, and relevance labels. Keep a simple dense-only and lexical-only baseline so a fused ranking can be judged against the evidence each component already finds.

query: What does this passage say about Candidate depth sets a ceiling for later ranking stages?
positive_text:
# Candidate depth sets a ceiling for later ranking stages

Fusion and reranking operate on candidates returned by earlier searches. If a relevant passage is below the retrieval cutoff, later stages cannot promote it. Increasing the cutoff may expose more relevant passages, but it also increases the work required for fusion, storage, or model-based reranking.

Tune candidate depth with a fixed query set. Measure whether relevant items enter the shortlist before spending time on reranker settings. If recall stops improving as depth grows, investigate indexing, query formulation, filters, and corpus coverage rather than assuming that a slower ranking model will find missing evidence.

query: What does this passage say about Rerank a shortlist instead of the whole corpus?
positive_text:
# Rerank a shortlist instead of the whole corpus

A reranker receives a query and a smaller set of retrieved passages, scores their relevance, and sorts that set again. A bi-encoder can embed each query and passage separately for efficient retrieval. A cross-encoder reads the query and candidate together, allowing a more direct relevance comparison at greater per-pair cost.

This division is useful when the corpus is too large to score every passage with a cross-encoder. The fast retriever creates a shortlist; the slower model refines its order. Reranking can improve precision at the top, but cannot add a passage that is absent from the shortlist.

Reference: [Sentence Transformers retrieve and rerank](https://sbert.net/examples/applications/retrieve_rerank/README.html); [Qdrant hybrid search with reranking](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/tutorials-basics/reranking-hybrid-search/).

query: What does this passage say about Interpreting cross-encoder scores?
positive_text:
# Interpreting cross-encoder scores

A cross-encoder score is a model output used to order query-passage pairs. Its numeric value is not automatically a calibrated probability, and scores from different reranker models may use different ranges. Ranking within a candidate set is often the intended use; a universal threshold requires calibration on representative labeled data.

A small shortlist controls inference cost because the model evaluates each query-passage pair. Track the number of candidates, model version, hardware, and latency alongside ranking quality. If the answer passage never reached the shortlist, a high score for another passage does not establish that the reranker is the cause of the miss.

query: What does this passage say about Vector collection query and lookup are different operations?
positive_text:
# Vector collection query and lookup are different operations

A vector query ranks records by similarity to a query embedding. A record lookup retrieves known IDs or filtered records without similarity ranking. Applications often need both: similarity search discovers candidate chunks, while lookup retrieves the stored text and metadata for selected chunk IDs.

Keep the query embedding dimension consistent with the collection. Store source identifiers and other citation metadata with each chunk, and request the fields needed by the next stage. A result can then carry its text, ID, and provenance together instead of requiring a separate guess about where it came from.

Reference: [Chroma Query and Get](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/querying-collections/query-and-get).

positive_text:
# Metadata filters narrow the searchable evidence

Metadata describes a record with fields such as source file, page, publication date, or document type. A filter can restrict a similarity query to records whose metadata meets a condition. A document-text filter can also search for text conditions, but it is not a substitute for semantic similarity ranking.

Filters are useful for user constraints such as “search only this folder” or “use documents from this year.” Validate filter keys and values before passing them to a storage backend. Keep the original metadata available in results so the report can cite the source and location that produced each claim.

Reference: [Chroma Query and Get](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/querying-collections/query-and-get).
negative_text:
# Chunk identifiers preserve citation provenance

Each indexed passage needs a stable identifier that connects it to its source text. Useful metadata includes the source path or URL, page when available, and character offsets in the extracted document. A citation ID should be deterministic for the same source and chunking settings so an evaluation set can continue to point to the same evidence.

When a report cites a chunk, validate that the ID exists in the evidence store. Resolve the ID to the stored text and metadata before the critic checks the claim. This turns a citation from decorative text into a verifiable link between a statement and the passage offered as support.

Reference: [Chroma Query and Get](https://docs.trychroma.com/docs/querying-collections/query-and-get); ARA corpus note, original text licensed under CC BY 4.0.

# A local chat endpoint keeps model choice configurable

Ollama exposes a chat endpoint that accepts a model name and a sequence of role/content messages. Its response includes an assistant message. The request can also include generation options, tool definitions, a response format, and a streaming preference.

An application should keep the endpoint URL, model name, timeout, and temperature in configuration. It should create its HTTP client only when a request is made, report endpoint errors clearly, and avoid treating a successful HTTP response as proof that the content is valid. Structured responses still need schema validation in the application.

Reference: [Ollama chat API](https://docs.ollama.com/api/chat).

query: What does this passage say about Streaming and structured output solve different problems?
positive_text:
# Streaming and structured output solve different problems

Streaming lets a client receive generated content in pieces before the full answer is complete. This can reduce perceived wait time for an interactive user, but the client must handle partial output and completion events. A final report pipeline may prefer a non-streaming call when it needs to validate the whole response before using it.

Structured output asks the model for data in a specified format, such as JSON or a JSON Schema. The application should still parse the result, validate it against its own schema, and retry or fail visibly when validation fails. A format request helps constrain generation; it does not replace validation.

Reference: [Ollama chat API](https://docs.ollama.com/api/chat); [Pydantic models and validation](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/models/).

query: What does this passage say about MCP separates the host, client, and server roles?
positive_text:
# MCP separates the host, client, and server roles

The Model Context Protocol uses a host-client-server structure. The host is the AI application coordinating work. It creates a client connection for each MCP server. A server offers context or operations to the connected client, and may run locally or remotely depending on its transport.

MCP standardizes context exchange; it does not decide how an application plans a report or what an LLM should do with returned data. Keeping those responsibilities separate lets the host use several independent servers while retaining its own policy for evidence selection, budgets, and report construction.

Reference: [MCP architecture overview](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/concepts/architecture). Documentation license: CC BY 4.0 for documentation contributions; specification content has separate licensing terms.
negative_text:
# MCP tools and resources have different control flows

An MCP tool is a callable operation that a model can request through the host. A resource is information the application can choose to load into context. A prompt is a reusable message template selected by a user or application. These roles matter because reading evidence and taking an action are different kinds of request.

Tool arguments should be validated at the server boundary, and tool output should be treated as data. The caller should check error indicators and validate returned fields before relying on them. A protocol connection provides a standard way to exchange messages, but the application still owns its trust and authorization rules.

query: What does this passage say about Training data and batches make reranker experiments reproducible?
positive_text:
# Training data and batches make reranker experiments reproducible

Supervised reranker training needs examples that pair a query with a passage and a relevance label. Positive passages should contain useful evidence for the query. Hard negatives should be plausible candidates that retrieval might return but that do not answer the query. Split by source document before training so near-duplicate passages from one document do not leak across train and test.

A dataset stores samples and labels; a data loader batches them for the training loop. Keep the seed, split IDs, model configuration, and checkpoint path with the run. Evaluate against fixed retrieval and ranking baselines using the same held-out query set.

positive_text:
# Retrieved text is evidence, not an instruction channel

Documents and web pages can contain text that looks like a command to the model. A research assistant should mark retrieved content as untrusted source material, keep system and developer instructions separate, and tell the model not to follow instructions embedded inside evidence. The application should also restrict which tools may be called and validate tool arguments independently.

This boundary does not make prompt injection impossible. It reduces confusion between the question, the agent's instructions, and the material being analyzed. Test with documents that contain hostile instructions, and confirm that the researcher summarizes their factual content without executing their requests.
negative_text:
# A retrieval pipeline for evidence-grounded answers

A retrieval-augmented answer has two stages. First, a retriever selects passages that may support the question. Second, a language model drafts an answer from those passages. The retrieved passages should remain attached to the answer so a reader can inspect the evidence. This keeps retrieval errors visible: a fluent paragraph does not prove that the right source was found.

For a small research assistant, keep the pipeline explicit: ingest source files, assign stable chunk IDs, retrieve a candidate set, optionally rerank it, and ask the writer to use only that evidence. If the candidate set is empty or does not support the requested detail, the system should say so instead of filling gaps from model memory.

# MCP separates the host, client, and server roles

The Model Context Protocol uses a host-client-server structure. The host is the AI application coordinating work. It creates a client connection for each MCP server. A server offers context or operations to the connected client, and may run locally or remotely depending on its transport.

MCP standardizes context exchange; it does not decide how an application plans a report or what an LLM should do with returned data. Keeping those responsibilities separate lets the host use several independent servers while retaining its own policy for evidence selection, budgets, and report construction.

negative_text:
# Streaming and structured output solve different problems

Streaming lets a client receive generated content in pieces before the full answer is complete. This can reduce perceived wait time for an interactive user, but the client must handle partial output and completion events. A final report pipeline may prefer a non-streaming call when it needs to validate the whole response before using it.

Structured output asks the model for data in a specified format, such as JSON or a JSON Schema. The application should still parse the result, validate it against its own schema, and retry or fail visibly when validation fails. A format request helps constrain generation; it does not replace validation.

Reference: [Ollama chat API](https://docs.ollama.com/api/chat); [Pydantic models and validation](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/models/).
